The story uses subtext extensively, and it naturally enriches both the emotional depth and the setting rather than feeling forced. 

On the surface, the story is about two people on a summer residency getting temporarily stranded on mud flats during an incoming tide. On the subtextual level, their physical environment mirrors their emotional state: they are two people used to living "temporary" lives who are avoiding talking about what happens "after" their residency ends. 

For example, when they walk out onto the mud flats, the narrator notes that they talked about the residency and the barns, "about everything except the thing, and both of us were aware of the thing the way you're aware of a fire alarm that hasn't gone off yet." The encroaching tide and their becoming "genuinely, physically, mutually stuck" on the sandbar serve as a natural metaphor for the unavoidable deadline of their departure and their growing feelings for one another. Similarly, their conversations about job offers in Iowa and auditions in Boston carry the unspoken weight of whether they will choose to stay in each other's lives. Because the characters are established as pragmatic, guarded adults ("competent adults do not make temporary situations into permanent problems"), their reliance on subtext and indirect dialogue feels completely authentic to who they are.
